oneIdea: Real measurements are noisy, so we do not force a curve through every point. Instead we choose the curve whose squared gaps to the data, \(S_r\), add up to the smallest possible number. The same idea fits a straight line, a curve after a log trick, or a polynomial, and \(r^2\) tells you how good the result is.
goals: Say the difference between regression (follow the trend of noisy data) and interpolation (hit every point).
Explain what the residual \(e_i\) and the sum of squares \(S_r\) are, and why we square the residuals.
Fit a straight line \(y=a_0+a_1x\) to a few points by hand using the slope and intercept formulas.
Compute \(S_t\), \(S_r\) and \(r^2\) and say what \(r^2\) does and does not tell you.
Turn \(y=ae^{bx}\) and \(y=ax^b\) into straight-line problems by taking logs, then undo the log.
Use MATLAB's polyfit and polyval to fit a line or a polynomial.

intro.idea: Curve fitting finds the trend in scattered data. The curve does not have to touch the points; it has to describe them well overall.
intro.mistake: Forcing a curve through every noisy point. That fits the measurement errors too and gives a wiggly, misleading curve.

check.q: Ten readings from a noisy sensor scatter around a rising trend. Which tool fits?
check.why: Noisy data call for regression, which follows the trend. Interpolation (Module 4) is for exact data.

best.idea: A residual is the vertical gap \(e_i=y_i-a_0-a_1x_i\). Least squares picks the line with the smallest \(S_r=\sum e_i^2\).
best.mistake: Minimizing the plain sum of residuals. Positive and negative gaps cancel, so a terrible line can still give a sum of 0.

check.q: A line leaves residuals \(3,\,-3,\,1,\,-1\). What is \(S_r\)?
check.why: Square first, then add: \(9+9+1+1=20\). The plain sum is 0, which is exactly why we square.

linear.idea: Two formulas give the best line: the slope \(a_1\) from the sums, then \(a_0=\bar y-a_1\bar x\), which forces the line through the centroid \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
linear.mistake: Computing \(a_0\) before \(a_1\). You need the slope first, because the intercept uses it.

check.q: The best line has slope \(a_1=3\), and the data have \(\bar x=2\), \(\bar y=5\). What is \(a_0\)?
check.why: \(a_0=\bar y-a_1\bar x=5-3(2)=-1\). Check: the line passes through \((2,5)\) since \(-1+3(2)=5\).

demo.idea: Drag or add points and watch the teal line move. The red stems are the residuals; the line settles where their squares add up to the least.
demo.mistake: Assuming one far-away point barely matters. Because gaps are squared, an outlier pulls the line toward itself a lot.

check.q: You switch the demo from a straight line to a quadratic on the same points. What happens to \(S_r\)?
opts: It can only go down or stay the same
check.why: A line is a quadratic with \(a_2=0\), so the best quadratic is at least as good as the best line.

error.idea: \(S_t\) is the spread about the mean, \(S_r\) the spread about the line. \(r^2=(S_t-S_r)/S_t\) is the fraction of the variation the line explains.
error.mistake: Treating a high \(r^2\) as proof the model is right. Always plot the residuals: a curve or fan shape in them means the model is wrong.

check.q: For some data \(S_t=10\) and \(S_r=2\). What is \(r^2\)?
check.why: \(r^2=(10-2)/10=0.8\). It must lie between 0 and 1, so 8 is impossible.

linz.idea: A log turns a curved model into a straight line. Fit the line to the transformed data, then transform the coefficients back.
linz.mistake: Forgetting to undo the log. For \(y=ax^b\) the intercept is \(\log a\), so \(a=10^{\text{intercept}}\), while \(b\) is the slope as it is.

check.q: Data follow \(y=3e^{2x}\). You plot \(\ln y\) against \(x\). What is the slope of the line?
check.why: \(\ln y=\ln 3+2x\), so the slope is \(b=2\) and the intercept is \(\ln 3\).

poly.idea: A polynomial fit is still linear in the unknown coefficients \(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_m\), so one matrix solve gives the answer.
poly.mistake: Thinking a curved model needs a hard non-linear method. \(y=a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2\) is curved in \(x\) but linear in the \(a\)'s.

check.q: How big is the normal-equation matrix for a cubic fit (degree \(m=3\))?
check.why: Degree \(m\) has \(m+1\) coefficients \(a_0,\dots,a_m\), so the matrix is \((m+1)\times(m+1)\): 4 by 4 for a cubic.

matlab.idea: p = polyfit(x,y,m) finds the coefficients and polyval(p,xq) evaluates the fit. Change m to change the degree.
matlab.mistake: Reading the output backwards. polyfit returns the highest power first, so a line gives [a1 a0], not [a0 a1].
